notes.title: Slide 9
notes.body: Introduction to Computer Hardware The physical elements that make up a computer system are called as the computer hardware. These parts work collectively to process, retailer and retrieve information serving the aim of a pc in order that it’s your job performs. Anyone who wants to build, repair or upgrade a computer should have at least an understanding of the key components of hardware since each serves its own purpose in the operation mode.

notes.title: Slide 10
notes.body: Computers have become indispensable in our everyday lives, and understanding their hardware components is crucial not only for building and repairing systems but also for optimizing their performance.

notes.title: Slide 11
notes.body: 1. Central Processing Unit (CPU): The Brain of the Computer The CPU is the "brain" of the computer, responsible for processing all instructions from software and hardware. It performs calculations, executes commands, and manages data flow between the different components. Modern CPUs have multiple cores, which allow them to perform several tasks simultaneously.

notes.title: Slide 14
notes.body: 2. The Motherboard: The Backbone of the Computer The motherboard is the main circuit board that holds the CPU, memory, and other essential components. It acts as the backbone of the computer, enabling communication between all hardware components through its slots, connectors, and circuits. It also contains the BIOS/UEFI firmware that helps initialize the hardware during boot-up.

notes.title: Slide 15
notes.body: It hosts the CPU, RAM, storage drives, and other essential components. It facilitates communication between the CPU and other components through buses, which are pathways that transfer data. The motherboard also contains the BIOS or UEFI, which is firmware that helps boot the computer and manage low-level operations.

notes.title: Slide 18
notes.body: 3. Random Access Memory (RAM): Temporary Storage for Data RAM is the computer’s temporary memory. It stores data that is currently being used by the CPU, allowing for quick access and smooth operation. When a computer is powered off, the data stored in RAM is lost. More RAM generally allows for better multitasking and faster performance. It is a form of volatile memory, meaning it only stores data while the computer is powered on:

notes.title: Slide 19
notes.body: When you open an application, data is loaded from the hard drive into RAM because RAM allows the CPU to access this data much faster. The more RAM yoursystem has, the more programs you can run simultaneously without slowing down. Unlike storage devices, data in RAM is erased when the system is turned off

notes.title: Slide 26
notes.body: 4. Storage Devices: Permanent Data Storage Computers store data permanently in storage devices like hard drives and solid-state drives. There are two primary types of storage devices

notes.title: Slide 27
notes.body: Hard Disk Drive (HDD): This use spinning magnetic platters to read and write data. They have been widely used for decades and offer large storage capacities at lower prices. Solid-State Drive (SSD): A newer storage technology that uses flash memory. It has no moving parts, making it faster, more reliable, and energy-efficient compared to HDDs. SSDs have become more popular due to their speed, which significantly reduces boot times and improves file access speeds.

notes.body: 5. Power Supply Unit (PSU): Providing Power to the System The Power Supply Unit converts electricity from your wall outlet into a form that can be used by the internal components of the computer. It distributes the correct voltage to various parts, including the motherboard, CPU, and storage devices

notes.title: Slide 32
notes.body: Function: Converts high-voltage alternating current (AC) from a wall outlet into low-voltage direct current (DC) for internal computer parts. Key Spec: Measured in watts (e.g., 550W, 750W, 850W); higher wattage supports stronger graphics cards and processors. Efficiency: Graded by the 80 Plus system (Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum) to show energy waste levels. Cabling: Available as non-modular, semi-modular, or fully modular for wire management.

notes.title: Slide 34
notes.body: The PSU's power output is measured in watts (W), and it must provide enough power to handle all the components. A higher wattage PSU is often required for systems with more demanding components like high-end GPUs or multiple hard drives.

notes.title: Slide 38
notes.body: 6. Graphics Processing Unit (GPU): For Visual Output The GPUis responsible for rendering images, videos, and animations on the monitor. While basic tasks like word processing rely on integrated graphics (which are built into the CPU), more graphically intensive tasks, such as gaming and video editing, require dedicated GPUs for better performance.

notes.title: Slide 39
notes.body: Integrated GPU: Built into the CPU, sufficient for basic tasks like web browsing and office work. Dedicated GPU: A separate graphics card used for more demanding tasks such as gaming, 3D rendering, and video editing.

notes.title: Slide 41
notes.body: 7. Cooling Systems(Fans and Heatsinks): Managing Heat Cooling systems (fans, heatsinks, and liquid coolers) ensure that the internal temperature stays within safe limits. Cooling systems prevent the CPU, GPU, and other components from overheating during operation. Heatsinks absorb and dissipate heat, while fans improve airflow within the case.

notes.title: Slide 42
notes.body: Fansandheatsinks dissipate heat from the CPU, GPU, and other components. High-performance systems may use liquid cooling to manage heat more effectively.

Output devices provide feedback from the computer: ● Monitor displays visual output. ● Speakers or headphones provide audio output. ● Printers produce physical copies of documents.

A DisplayPort transmits digital video and audio (not analog transmissions) and is slowly replacing VGA and DVI ports on personal computers. A Thunderbolt port transmits both video and data on the same port and cable. lessons.description: Original source wording, fixed term questions, and complete coverage.

notes.title: Slide 3
notes.body: System administration is a job done by Information Technology experts for an organization. The job is to ensure that computer systems and all related services are working well. Provide support services Ensure reliable operations Promote efficient use of the system Ensures that prescribe service-quality objectives met

notes.title: Slide 4
notes.body: What does a system administrator do? Managing Windows, Linux, or Mac systems Upgrading, installing, and configuring application software and computer hardware Troubleshooting and providing technical support to employees Creating and managing system permissions and user accounts Performing regular security tests and security monitoring Maintaining networks and network file systems

notes.title: Slide 5
notes.body: SYSTEM ADMINISTRATOR The system administrator, IT system administrator, system administrator, or sys admin is a person employed to manage and maintain a computer system and/or a network.

notes.title: Slide 6
notes.body: The term ADMINISTRATOR can have several different meanings. In a company or organization, he or she is the person who ensures that everything operates efficiently . Their specific duties depend on the type of company, organization, or entity where there work. In business, the ADMINISTRATOR is the person in charge of BUSINESS ADMINISTRATION . They manage the company’s finance, human resources, marketing, accounting and business operation

notes.title: Slide 7
notes.body: DIFFERENT TYPE OF ADMINISTRATOR DATABASE ADMINISTRATOR NETWORK ADMINISTRATOR SECURITY SYSTEM ADMINISTRATOR SERVER/WEB ADMINISTRATOR

notes.title: Slide 8
notes.body: Most companies are filling other positions related to system administration . Within a larger organization, most of these may be separate positions within the Technical Support or Information Services (IS) department.

notes.title: Slide 9
notes.body: DATABASE ADMINISTRATOR

notes.title: Slide 10
notes.body: The Database Administrator (DBA) manages a database infrastructure and is responsible for data integrity and infrastructure reliability and accuracy.

notes.title: Slide 11
notes.body: Database administrators maintain and protect sensitive information and provide access to important datasets for companies, institutions, and government bodies. Database administrators also back up, restore, and troubleshoot database sets and system access, updating and integrating old programs to implement the latest technology. What Does a Database Administrator Do?

notes.title: Slide 12
notes.body: Key Hard Skills SQL: SQL, a computer language, orients and organizes all data management systems. Database administrator should understand the three dominant database languages: Microsoft SQL, Oracle Database, and IBM's DB2. UNIX: This portable, multi-user, multitasking operating system interface is made available by The Open Group. Linux: Modeled after UNIX, the open-source operating system Linux operates with versatility to control a variety of computer systems, including smartphones and supercomputers.

notes.title: Slide 13
notes.body: Oracle: A relational database framework oriented through SQL, Oracle provides access to and organizes datasets. Windows Operating System: Windows OS represents the orienting graphic interface for all Microsoft products. Data Analysis: By inspecting, collating, and interpreting datasets, data analysts translate massive bodies of information into useful and illustrative material for companies and clients. Microsoft Access: This is the key information management tool behind referencing, reporting, and data analysis in data administration. MS Access translates metadata sets, particularly from Microsoft Excel sheets, into usable, searchable datasets. HTML: HTML, or Hypertext Markup Language, forms the graphics of platform and website design. Professionals create interactive systems and webpages using this standard coding language, which integrates scripting languages such as JavaScript.

notes.title: Slide 14
notes.body: Key Soft Skills of database administrator Analytics: The ability to systematically analyze data or statistics helps database administrators identify and meet their companies' data management needs. Database administrators often conduct updated analyses of their databases, as well. Business-Focused: Companies trust database administrators to make cost-effective decisions regarding technology and staff for data storage, maintenance, security, and analysis. Technical and business knowledge and skills make database administrators more valuable and versatile. Communication: Database administrators often supervise other IT staff, and good communication skills prove valuable to IT teamwork and leadership. Database administrators also communicate with executive management, suppliers, and technology professionals at other organizations.

notes.title: Slide 15
notes.body: Problem-solving: The capacity to identify, test, and eliminate potential problems and their causes is extremely valuable to database administrators, who spend a considerable amount of time troubleshooting. Organization: Databases require considerable organization, and database administrators organize data to make database decisions and create reports. They also organize IT department tasks and employees.

notes.title: Slide 16
notes.body: NETWORK ADMINISTRATOR

notes.title: Slide 17
notes.body: The network administrator manages network equipment, such as switches and routers, and detects issues with or with the actions of computers linked to the network.

notes.title: Slide 18
notes.body: What does a network administrator do? Install, configure, and maintain network hardware and software such as routers, firewalls, and switches Protect networks from unauthorized users through physical and technical means Set up and maintain virtual private networks (VPN) Resolve network connectivity issues for other employees Maintain and troubleshoot storage networks

notes.title: Slide 19
notes.body: How to become a network administrator As a network specialist, you’ll want to have a knowledge of basic networking skills. A networking certification can help you gain necessary skills and show employers your capabilities. You can also get your start in help desk roles and work your way up to being a network administrator.

notes.title: Slide 20
notes.body: Key network administrator skills 1 . Knowledge of different types of networks: Local Area Networks (LANs) Wide Area Networks (WANs), Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), and sometimes Storage Area Networks (SANs) are each different types of networks.

notes.title: Slide 21
notes.body: 2. Understanding of network security components: These might include firewalls, VPNs, and access control. Knowing what common attacks are and the appropriate response to them will be important as a network administrator.

notes.title: Slide 22
notes.body: 3. Familiarity with servers: Upgrading and configuring servers is a common ability sought after in network administrators. Windows and Linux servers are common

notes.title: Slide 23
notes.body: 4. Communication and teamwork: As a network administrator, you’ll likely be working in a team or with other members of your organization to ensure computers and systems are up and running. Being able to communicate problems and solutions with other people is a valuable skill to have.

notes.title: Slide 24
notes.body: System administration vs. network administration?

notes.title: Slide 25
notes.body: SECURITY ADMINISTRATOR

notes.title: Slide 26
notes.body: The security administrator is a computer and network security expert, performing the management of security devices like firewalls, as well as general security consultations.

notes.title: Slide 27
notes.body: What Does a Security Administrator Do Security administrators fill one of the most crucial roles in information technology (IT). They oversee many responsibilities to ensure their organizations' computer networks and systems remain secure.

notes.title: Slide 28
notes.body: Without proper security measures, organizations remain susceptible to cyberattacks from hackers , terrorist organizations , and foreign governments , who often aim to steal data or money . In some cases, cyberattacks infiltrate an organization's computer network, lock users out, and demand ransom money.

notes.title: Slide 29
notes.body: These professionals develop policies, systems, and technologies to protect their companies' and customers' sensitive data. They may implement regulations to govern how information travels between employees and outside the office.

notes.title: Slide 30
notes.body: security administrators work in teams to identify their networks' weak points and install firewalls, site-blocking programs, and anti-malware software. Security administrators may also handle responses to unwanted intrusions.

notes.title: Slide 31
notes.body: Key Soft Skills for Security Administrators Communication : security administrators must be able to speak the professional languages of app developers, IT team members, and business management professionals. Critical Thinking : Security administrators must apply problem-solving methodologies and technology theories to new problems as they arise. Continuous Learning : To progress in their careers, security administrators need to be lifelong learners. Calm Under Stress : Like other cybersecurity professionals, security administrators often work under pressure in a closely monitored environment.

notes.title: Slide 32
notes.body: Key Hard Skills for Security Administrators Vulnerability Assessment : Security administrators must be able to determine when a pattern of activity differs from typical operations. Identity Management : Security administrators authorize and manage employees' online identities, allowing the right people to access the right information at the right time Intrusion Detection : These professionals flag and address suspicious activities. They should know how to use network intrusion and host intrusion detection systems Risk Management : Security administrators identify, evaluate, and address security threats. Administrators should also use select solutions to prevent cybersecurity breaches.

notes.title: Slide 33
notes.body: WEB/SERVER ADMINISTRATOR

notes.title: Slide 34
notes.body: A web administrator maintains web server services (such as Apache or IIS) that allow internal or external access to web pages. Tasks involve managing multiple websites, managing security, and installing the required components and software. Duties can also require the management of software changes.

notes.title: Slide 35
notes.body: What does a website administrator do? Automates and oversees sight deployment and development Web administrators oversee the deployment and development of new websites and create automated tools and processes. This might include using software to automatically publish blogs at certain times or using social media management software to schedule site posts and shares.

notes.title: Slide 36
notes.body: Oversees website security and connectivity The website administrator also oversees the website's security infrastructure and connectivity to the site server and web. Administrators help combat common cybersecurity threats like phishing attacks, bot attacks and brute force password attacks for website users.

notes.title: Slide 37
notes.body: Maintains and secures the website database Each website has a database of user, site and security data. The website administrator oversees the maintenance and security of the website database, erasing, adding or modifying data stored on the database.

notes.title: Slide 38
notes.body: Replies to website help desk requests Some website administrators act as the help desk for the site's users. If there's a problem with the website's connectivity, security or functionality, the website administrator investigates the issue and implements a solution.

notes.title: Slide 39
notes.body: important skills for website administrators: Coding skills: Web administrators typically have advanced coding skills and understand one or more coding languages for programming websites. Database skills: Administrators understand how a website's database works, how to secure it and what information to keep in the database. Project management skills: Web administrators can organise their time and resources to be efficient with strong project management skills. Teamwork skills: Administrators often work as part of a website development or technical support team, requiring teamwork skills like communication, active listening and collaboration

notes.title: Slide 40
notes.body: Computer skills: Website administrators are proficient with computers, computer software and computer troubleshooting. Web design skills: Administrators typically have excellent web design skills and understand the aesthetics and functionality of a good website. Management skills: Administrators manage entire websites and databases and a team of professionals, requiring strong management skills like communication, coaching and mentoring. Organisational skills: Administrators typically have strong organisational skills to organise their time, different projects, extensive web data and their team.

notes.title: Slide 41
notes.body: BASIC SKILLS Operating System Application Hardware Software / Hardware Troubleshooting Programming Language Computer Security

notes.title: Slide 42
notes.body: DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES OF A SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION system or software inspections. Performing data backups. Apply updates to the operating system and adjust settings. Installation and configuration of new hardware or software. Add / delete / create / modify user account information, reset passwords, etc.

notes.title: Slide 43
notes.body: Responding to technical questions. Responsible for security. Responsible for documenting the system setup. Troubleshooting any identified issues or problems. Keep the network up and running.

notes.title: Slide 44
notes.body: System administrator jobs: If you're transitioning into IT from a related career or considering starting down the path to system administration, these jobs can serve as stepping stones to your goal and prepare you for success in your first role as a system administrator. Help desk technician IT support specialist Network analyst Computer systems analyst

notes.title: Slide 3
notes.body: OBJECTIVES Identify What Network and System Administration do Applying Technology in Environment Define the human role in the System Challenge of System Administration

notes.title: Slide 4
notes.body: What Network and System Administration? Network and system administration is a branch of engineering that concerns the operational management of human–computer systems. A system administrator works for users so that they can use the system to produce work. However, a system administrator should not just cater to one or two selfish needs but also work for the benefit of a whole community.

notes.title: Slide 5
notes.body: What is Network and System Administration? In the future, improvements in technology might render system administration a somewhat easier task – one of pure resource administration – but, today, system administration is not just an administrative job, it is an extremely demanding engineer’s job. It’s about hardware , software , user support , diagnosis , repair and prevention .

notes.title: Slide 7
notes.body: Applying technology in an environment The key task of network and system administration is to build hardware configurations, another is to configure software systems. Both of these tasks are performed for users. Hardware has to conform to the constraints of the physical world it requires power, a temperate (usually indoor) climate, and conformance to basic standards in order to work systematically

notes.title: Slide 8
notes.body: The Human role in systems For humans, the task of system administration is a balancing act. It requires Patience , Understanding , Knowledge and Experience . It is like working in the casualty ward of a hospital. Administrators need to be the doctor, the psychologist, and – when instruments fail – the mechanic.

notes.title: Slide 9
notes.body: The challenges of system administration • Designing a network that is logical and efficient. • Deploying large numbers of machines that can be easily upgraded later. • Deciding what services are needed. • Planning and implementing adequate security. • Providing a comfortable environment for users. • Developing ways of fixing errors and problems which occur. • Keeping track of and understanding how to use the enormous amount of knowledge which increases every year.

notes.title: Slide 10
notes.body: The challenges of system administration System administration is not just about installing operating systems. It is about planning and designing an efficient community of computers so that real users will be able to get their jobs done .

notes.title: Slide 11
notes.body: Some system administrators are responsible for both the hardware of the network and the computers which it connects, the cables as well as the computers. Some are only responsible for the computers. Either way, an understanding of how data flow from machine to machine is essential as well as an understanding of how each machine affects every other

notes.title: Slide 12
notes.body: Ethical issues A system administrator has many responsibilities and constraints to consider. Ethically, the first responsibility must be to the greater network community, and then to the users of our system. An administrator’s job is to make users’ lives bearable and to empower them in the production of real work

notes.title: Slide 13
notes.body: Computer ethics “Computer ethics deals with the procedures, values, and practices that govern the process of consuming computing technology and its related disciplines without damaging or violating the moral values and beliefs of any individual, organization, or entity.”

notes.title: Page 3
notes.body: What is Diagnostics? Diagnostics is the process of investigating a problem to determine its cause. It involves collecting information, examining system behavior, analyzing available evidence, and identifying the component or condition responsible for the problem. For example, when a website becomes inaccessible, the cause may be a network problem, server failure, database issue, software error, or incorrect configuration. Diagnostics helps determine which of these is actually responsible.

notes.title: Page 4
notes.body: Diagnostic Process A diagnostic process usually begins by identifying the symptom and collecting relevant information. The information is then analyzed to determine the likely cause. After a solution is applied, the system must be checked again to confirm that the problem has actually been resolved.

notes.title: Page 5
notes.body: diagnostic process 2.Collect Information 1.Identify Problem 3.Analyze Evidence 4.Identify Cause 5.Apply Solution 6.Verify Result

notes.title: Page 6
notes.body: Diagnostic Tools and Information IT professionals use different sources of information when diagnosing a problem. These may include system logs, error messages, monitoring data, network information, performance statistics, configuration records, and user reports. The information collected depends on the type of problem being investigated. The purpose is to gather enough evidence to distinguish the actual cause from possible causes.

notes.title: Page 7
notes.body: SYSTEM LOGS ERROR MESSAGES MONITORING NETWORK STATUS PERFORMANCE D A T A U S E R REPORTS IT INVESTIGATION KIT

notes.title: Page 8
notes.body: diagnostics example A university enrollment website suddenly becomes unavailable. Instead of immediately restarting the server, the IT team checks the server status, application logs, database connection, network connectivity, and recent system activity. The investigation shows that the database server has reached its storage capacity. The website problem was therefore caused by a database storage issue rather than the network.

notes.title: Page 9
notes.body: What is a Fault? A fault is a condition or defect that causes an IT component or system to operate incorrectly. It may occur in hardware, software, networks, databases, or system configurations. Examples include a damaged network cable, failed server component, corrupted database, incorrect configuration, or insufficient storage. A fault is the underlying condition, while a failure is the resulting loss of function or service.

notes.title: Page 10
notes.body: fault management Fault management involves detecting, isolating, diagnosing, correcting, and monitoring faults in an IT environment. Its main purpose is to restore normal system operation while minimizing the impact on users. Once a fault is identified, the IT team determines the appropriate corrective action and verifies that the service has returned to normal.

notes.title: Page 11
notes.body: 1 2 3 4 5 6 how to find the fault Detect Fault Isolate Fault Diagnose Correct Restore Service Monitor

notes.title: Page 12
notes.body: A school's online registration system becomes extremely slow. The network appears to be functioning normally, so the IT team checks the server. The investigation shows that the server's storage is almost completely full because of accumulated temporary files and logs. The team safely removes unnecessary data, restores available storage, and monitors system performance. The example shows why the visible symptom does not always identify the actual fault. Fault Management Example

notes.title: Page 13
notes.body: Fault Resolution Correcting a fault restores the system, but the team should also consider whether the same problem could happen again. For example, repeatedly deleting files whenever storage becomes full may solve the immediate problem but does not address why storage continues to reach its limit. The organization may eventually need additional storage, automated monitoring, or a change in its data- management practices.

notes.title: Page 14
notes.body: Delete files TEMPORARY FIX LONG-TERM SOLUTION Increase storage Restart System Investigate recurring cause Restore service Add monitoring which is better?

notes.title: Page 15
notes.body: What is Change Management? Change management is the controlled process of planning, assessing, approving, implementing, and reviewing changes to an IT environment. Changes may include software updates, database modifications, server replacement, network configuration changes, or security updates. The purpose is to introduce necessary changes while reducing the possibility of service disruption, errors, data loss, or other unintended effects.

notes.title: Page 16
notes.body: Change Management Process A change should be planned before it is implemented. The organization first identifies what needs to change and why. The possible impact and risks are then considered, followed by the required authorization and implementation planning. After the change is performed, the system is tested and monitored to determine whether the intended result was achieved.

notes.title: Page 17
notes.body: Approval Planning Implementation Testing Review Change Request Assessment

notes.title: Page 18
notes.body: Why is Change Management Important? An IT change can improve a system, but it can also introduce new problems if it is poorly planned. For example, a software update may create compatibility issues, a database modification may affect applications, or a network configuration change may interrupt connectivity. Change management helps organizations consider these risks before implementation and prepare appropriate recovery measures.

notes.title: Page 19
notes.body: example of change management A university needs to increase the database storage of its enrollment system because the existing capacity is almost full. Instead of changing the database immediately, the IT team evaluates the impact, prepares a backup, obtains approval, schedules the activity, and prepares a recovery plan. After increasing the storage, the team tests the enrollment system and monitors its performance. This demonstrates how a technical solution becomes a controlled change.

notes.title: Page 20
notes.body: 1 types of change Standard Change A routine and well-understood change that follows an established procedure.

notes.title: Page 21
notes.body: 2 types of change Normal Change A change that requires assessment and authorization before implementation.

notes.title: Page 22
notes.body: 3 types of change Emergency Change An urgent change performed to address a critical situation where waiting for the normal process could create greater risk.

notes.title: Page 23
notes.body: Change Verification Completing the technical change does not automatically mean that the change was successful. The organization must verify that the system works as expected and determine whether the change created any unexpected effects. Implement Change → Test → Monitor → Review → Confirm Success Testing, monitoring, documentation, and review help determine whether the change achieved its intended purpose.

notes.title: Page 24
notes.body: Diagnostics, Fault Management, and Change Management These three processes address different stages of handling an IT problem. Diagnostics determines what is happening and helps identify the cause. Fault Management focuses on correcting the fault and restoring normal service. Change Management controls modifications that are required to improve the system or prevent similar problems from recurring.

notes.title: Page 25
notes.body: Case Study: University Enrollment System During enrollment, students report that the university portal is extremely slow. Diagnostics shows that the database server is almost out of storage. Fault management is used to restore the service by safely removing unnecessary temporary data and monitoring the server. Because the same issue has happened several times, the organization considers a permanent change. The team plans a storage expansion, evaluates its impact, creates a backup, obtains approval, implements the change, and verifies the system afterward.

notes.title: Page 26
notes.body: How the Three Processes Work Together A reliable IT response does not stop when the system starts working again. Diagnostics provides the information needed to understand the problem. Fault management helps restore normal operation, while change management provides a controlled way to modify the system when a longer-term solution is needed. The three processes can therefore be viewed as a continuous cycle: Investigate → Restore → Improve → Verify

notes.title: Page 3
notes.body: What is a Networked Community? A networked community is a group of people, devices, computer systems, and digital services that are connected through a network to communicate, share information, access resources, and collaborate with one another. In a networked community, users may connect through computers, smartphones, servers, cloud platforms, or other network- enabled devices. These connections allow information and services to move between different users and systems efficiently.

notes.title: Page 4
notes.body: How It Works People use the network to communicate and access shared resources. Devices such as computers, smartphones, and servers connect users to the network. Systems manage data, accounts, applications, and network operations. Services such as file sharing, email, websites, databases, and cloud storage provide resources to users. Networks connect all of these elements and allow them to exchange information.

notes.title: Page 5
notes.body: Simple Example A university network is a networked community because students, teachers, staff, computers, servers, Wi-Fi, online learning platforms, and shared resources are all connected and interact through the same network environment.

notes.title: Page 6
notes.body: Types of Networked Communities Networked communities can exist in different environments depending on their purpose and users. Educational Networks – Connect students, teachers, laboratories, and learning systems. Business Networks – Connect employees, departments, servers, and company resources. Government Networks – Support communication and information sharing between government offices.

notes.title: Page 7
notes.body: Types of Networked Communities Online Communities – Connect people through social media, forums, gaming platforms, and discussion groups. Cloud-Based Communities – Allow users to access shared applications and data through the internet.

notes.title: Page 8
notes.body: Key Characteristics of Networked Communities CONNECTIVITY Devices and users are linked through wired or wireless networks, allowing them to exchange data and access shared services. COMMUNICATION Users and systems can send and receive information through email, messaging platforms, video conferencing, and other network-based tools.

notes.title: Page 9
notes.body: Key Characteristics of Networked Communities RESOURCE SHARING Members can share files, printers, applications, storage, databases, and internet access across the network. COLLABORATION Networked communities allow multiple users to work together on projects, documents, and tasks even when they are in different locations.

notes.title: Page 10
notes.body: Key Characteristics of Networked Communities CENTRALIZED OR DECENTRALIZED MANAGEMENT Networks may be controlled from a central server or managed across several connected systems depending on the organization’s structure. ACCESSIBI LITY Authorized users can access information and services from different devices and locations, depending on the network's permissions and security settings.

Mobile Data – Uses cellular networks such as 4G and 5G. People and devices can connect to networked communities usingdifferent technologies.

notes.title: Page 16
notes.body: Challenges of Networked Communities Network Downtime Users may temporarily lose access to systems and services. Cybersecurity Threats Malware, unauthorized access, and other attacks can affect systems. Privacy Concerns Personal and organizational information must be properly protected.

notes.title: Page 17
notes.body: Challenges of Networked Communities Technical Problems Hardware, software, or configuration problems can interrupt services. Dependence on Connectivity Some services become unavailable when the network or internetconnection fails.

notes.title: Page 18
notes.body: A system administrator, or sysadmin, is the person responsible formanaging and maintaining an organization’s computer systems andnetwork. In a networked community, the system administrator makes surethat users can access the systems they need, while keeping the networkreliable and secure. Your presentation identifies responsibilities such asmanaging user accounts and permissions, maintaining servers andnetwork services, installing and configuring systems, monitoringperformance, troubleshooting problems, protecting systems fromthreats, and handling backup and recovery. notes.title: Page 19
notes.body: Responsibilities of a System Administrator in Networked Community User Management – Manages accounts, roles, and access permissions. Server Management – Maintains servers and network services. Installation & Configuration – Installation & Configuration – Sets up hardware, software, andsystems.

notes.title: Page 20
notes.body: Responsibilities of a System Administrator in Networked Community Monitoring & Maintenance – Checks system performance and keeps systems updated. Troubleshooting – Identifies and resolves technical problems. Security – Protects systems, users, and data from threats. Backup & Recovery – Creates backups and restores data when needed.

Data Loss Restores files and systems from backups.
